claim: Rodent visual cortex is organized in two clusters of strongly reciprocally connected areas, which resemble, anatomically, the primate ventral and dorsal streams.
source: Converging evidence (Wang and Burkhalter, 2007; Wang et al., 2011, 2012) indicates that rodent visual cortex is organized in two clusters of strongly reciprocally connected areas, which resemble, anatomically, the primate ventral and dorsal streams (i.e., the cortical pathways specialized for the processing of, respectively, shape and motion information).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies (Wang and Burkhalter, 2007; Wang et al., 2011, 2012).

claim: The first cluster of rodent visual areas includes most of lateral extrastriate areas, while the second encompasses medial and parietal extrastriate cortex.
source: The first cluster includes most of lateral extrastriate areas, while the second encompasses medial and parietal extrastriate cortex.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact following from the anatomical organization described in the previous sentence, which is supported by citations.

claim: Lesioning laterotemporal cortex strongly impairs visual pattern discrimination in rodents.
source: Solid causal evidence confirms the involvement of these modules in ventral-like and dorsal-like computations – lesioning laterotemporal and posterior parietal cortex strongly impairs, respectively, visual pattern discrimination and visuospatial perception (Gallardo et al., 1979; McDaniel et al., 1982; Wörtwein et al., 1993; Aggleton et al., 1997; Sánchez et al., 1997; Tees, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to lesion studies (Gallardo et al., 1979; McDaniel et al., 1982; Wörtwein et al., 1993; Aggleton et al., 1997; Sánchez et al., 1997; Tees, 1999).

claim: Lesioning posterior parietal cortex strongly impairs visuospatial perception in rodents.
source: Solid causal evidence confirms the involvement of these modules in ventral-like and dorsal-like computations – lesioning laterotemporal and posterior parietal cortex strongly impairs, respectively, visual pattern discrimination and visuospatial perception (Gallardo et al., 1979; McDaniel et al., 1982; Wörtwein et al., 1993; Aggleton et al., 1997; Sánchez et al., 1997; Tees, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to lesion studies (Gallardo et al., 1979; McDaniel et al., 1982; Wörtwein et al., 1993; Aggleton et al., 1997; Sánchez et al., 1997; Tees, 1999).

claim: Dorsal areas in rodent visual cortex are specialized for motion processing.
source: While studies employing parametric visual stimuli (e.g., drifting gratings) support the specialization of dorsal areas for motion processing (Andermann et al., 2011; Marshel et al., 2011; Juavinett and Callaway, 2015), the functional signature of ventral-like computations has yet to be found in lateral areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to functional studies (Andermann et al., 2011; Marshel et al., 2011; Juavinett and Callaway, 2015).

claim: Rats are capable of invariant recognition of visual objects.
source: Recently, a number of behavioral studies have shown that rats too are capable of invariant recognition (Zoccolan et al., 2009; Tafazoli et al., 2012; Vermaercke and Op de Beeck, 2012; Alemi-Neissi et al., 2013; Vinken et al., 2014; Rosselli et al., 2015), thus arguing for the existence of cortical machinery supporting this function also in rodents.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to behavioral studies (Zoccolan et al., 2009; Tafazoli et al., 2012; Vermaercke and Op de Beeck, 2012; Alemi-Neissi et al., 2013; Vinken et al., 2014; Rosselli et al., 2015).

claim: Rodents preferentially rely on vision during spatial navigation.
source: This hypothesis is further supported by the preferential reliance of rodents on vision during spatial navigation (Cushman et al., 2013; Zoccolan, 2015), and by the strong dependence of head-directional tuning on visual cues in rat hippocampus (Acharya et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on spatial navigation (Cushman et al., 2013; Zoccolan, 2015).

claim: Head-directional tuning in rat hippocampus strongly depends on visual cues.
source: This hypothesis is further supported by the preferential reliance of rodents on vision during spatial navigation (Cushman et al., 2013; Zoccolan, 2015), and by the strong dependence of head-directional tuning on visual cues in rat hippocampus (Acharya et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study on hippocampal head-directional tuning (Acharya et al., 2016).

claim: 771 visually driven and stimulus informative units were recorded across 26 rats: 228 from V1, 131 from LM, 260 from LI, and 152 from LL.
source: We recorded 771 visually driven and stimulus informative units in 26 rats: 228 from V1, 131 from LM, 260 from LI, and 152 from LL (neurons in each area came from at least eight rats; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: Neurons in each visual area came from at least eight rats.
source: We recorded 771 visually driven and stimulus informative units in 26 rats: 228 from V1, 131 from LM, 260 from LI, and 152 from LL (neurons in each area came from at least eight rats; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental design and data collection.

claim: The sparseness of neuronal firing across 230 stimulus conditions was not statistically different between LL and V1 populations.
source: Note that, although the example LL neuron of Figure 2D fired more sparsely than the example V1 neuron of Figure 2C, the sparseness of neuronal firing across the 230 stimulus conditions, measured as defined in (Vinje and Gallant, 2000), was not statistically different between the LL and the V1 populations (p>0.05; Mann-Whitney U-test), with the median sparseness being ~0.13 in both areas.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney U-test) of the experimental data.

claim: The median sparseness of neuronal firing was approximately 0.13 in both V1 and LL.
source: Note that, although the example LL neuron of Figure 2D fired more sparsely than the example V1 neuron of Figure 2C, the sparseness of neuronal firing across the 230 stimulus conditions, measured as defined in (Vinje and Gallant, 2000), was not statistically different between the LL and the V1 populations (p>0.05; Mann-Whitney U-test), with the median sparseness being ~0.13 in both areas.
evidence: This is a direct report of the measured sparseness values from the experimental data.

claim: The overall amount of visual information decreased gradually and significantly along the V1-LM-LI-LL progression.
source: The overall amount of visual information decreased gradually and significantly along the areas' progression (full bars in Figure 3B), with the median I(R;S) being about half in LL (~0.06 bits) than in V1 (~0.12 bits; 1-tailed, Mann-Whitney U-test, Holm-Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons; hereafter, unless otherwise stated, all the between-area comparisons have been statistically assessed with this test; see Material and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The median total stimulus information I(R;S) was about 0.06 bits in LL and about 0.12 bits in V1.
source: The overall amount of visual information decreased gradually and significantly along the areas' progression (full bars in Figure 3B), with the median I(R;S) being about half in LL (~0.06 bits) than in V1 (~0.12 bits; 1-tailed, Mann-Whitney U-test, Holm-Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons; hereafter, unless otherwise stated, all the between-area comparisons have been statistically assessed with this test; see Material and methods).
evidence: This is a direct report of the measured information values from the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The loss of energy-related stimulus information and the increase of transformation tolerance across the V1-LI-LL progression were found across the whole cortical thickness.
source: The loss of energy-related stimulus information and the increase of transformation tolerance across the V1-LI-LL progression were found: (1) across the whole cortical thickness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6C);
evidence: The claim is supported by the analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6C.

claim: The loss of energy-related stimulus information and the increase of transformation tolerance across the V1-LI-LL progression were found after matching the RF sizes of the four populations.
source: The loss of energy-related stimulus information and the increase of transformation tolerance across the V1-LI-LL progression were found: (1) across the whole cortical thickness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6C); (2) after matching the RF sizes of the four populations (Figure 7C–D);
evidence: The claim is supported by the analyses shown in Figure 7C–D.

claim: The loss of energy-related stimulus information and the increase of transformation tolerance across the V1-LI-LL progression were found across the whole spectrum of spike isolation quality.
source: The loss of energy-related stimulus information and the increase of transformation tolerance across the V1-LI-LL progression were found: (1) across the whole cortical thickness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6C); (2) after matching the RF sizes of the four populations (Figure 7C–D); (3) across the whole spectrum of spike isolation quality in our recordings (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B);
evidence: The claim is supported by the analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: The loss of energy-related stimulus information and the increase of transformation tolerance across the V1-LI-LL progression were found when considering only neuronal subpopulations with the best spike isolation quality.
source: The loss of energy-related stimulus information and the increase of transformation tolerance across the V1-LI-LL progression were found: (1) across the whole cortical thickness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 6C); (2) after matching the RF sizes of the four populations (Figure 7C–D); (3) across the whole spectrum of spike isolation quality in our recordings (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B); and (4) when considering only neuronal subpopulations with the best spike isolation quality (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), which also equated them in terms of firing rate (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analyses shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The linear separability of object representations at the single-neuron level increased monotonically and significantly along the V1-LM-LI-LL progression.
source: The linear separability of object representations at the single-neuron level increased monotonically and significantly along the areas' progression (Figure 5B), being ~4 times larger in LL as in V1 and LM, and reaching an intermediate value in LI.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5B and statistical testing.

claim: Linear separability at the single-neuron level was approximately 4 times larger in LL than in V1 and LM.
source: The linear separability of object representations at the single-neuron level increased monotonically and significantly along the areas' progression (Figure 5B), being ~4 times larger in LL as in V1 and LM, and reaching an intermediate value in LI.
evidence: This is a direct report of the measured linear separability values from the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The fraction of invariant information that was linearly decodable increased from approximately 55% in V1 to approximately 70% in LL.
source: To quantify this observation we computed, for each cell, the ratio between linear separability (Figure 5B) and amount of invariant information (Figure 4C, right). The resulting fraction of invariant information that was linearly decodable increased from ~55% in V1 to ~70% in LL, being significantly larger in LL than in any other area (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 5C and statistical testing.

claim: The ability of rat visual neurons to support generalization to novel object views increased as significantly and steeply as linear separability at the single-cell level.
source: Our analysis revealed that, when assessed at the single-cell level, the ability of rat visual neurons to support generalization to novel object views increased as significantly and steeply as linear separability (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6B and statistical testing.

claim: The growth of transformation tolerance from V1 to LL was widespread across the whole cortical thickness and equally sharp in superficial and deep layers.
source: Interestingly, this trend was widespread across the whole cortical thickness and equally sharp in superficial and deep layers, although the generalization performances were larger in the latter (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6C and statistical testing (two-way ANOVA).

claim: Generalization performances were larger in deep layers than in superficial layers.
source: Interestingly, this trend was widespread across the whole cortical thickness and equally sharp in superficial and deep layers, although the generalization performances were larger in the latter (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: RF size grew significantly at each step along the V1-LM-LI-LL progression.
source: Our recordings confirmed and expanded these previous observations, showing that RF size (defined in Materials and methods) grew significantly at each step along the areas' progression (Figure 7A), with the median in LL (~30° of visual angle) being about twice as large as in V1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7A and statistical testing.

claim: The median RF size in LL was approximately 30° of visual angle, about twice as large as in V1.
source: Our recordings confirmed and expanded these previous observations, showing that RF size (defined in Materials and methods) grew significantly at each step along the areas' progression (Figure 7A), with the median in LL (~30° of visual angle) being about twice as large as in V1.
evidence: This is a direct report of the measured RF size values from the experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When neuronal subpopulations with matched RF size ranges were considered, LL and LI afforded significantly larger tolerance than V1 and LM.
source: This allowed sampling the largest possible V1, LM, LI and LL subpopulations with matched RF size ranges (gray patches in Figure 7B), and computing the generalization performances yielded by these subpopulations (Figure 7C) – again, LL and LI afforded significantly larger tolerance than V1 and LM.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7C and statistical testing.

claim: In LI and LL, generalization performance and RF size were significantly anti-correlated.
source: While in V1 performance slightly increased as a function of RF size (although not significantly; p>0.05; two-tailed t-test), performance and RF size were significantly anti-correlated in LI and LL (p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7B and statistical testing (two-tailed t-test).

claim: In V1, generalization performance slightly increased as a function of RF size, although not significantly.
source: While in V1 performance slightly increased as a function of RF size (although not significantly; p>0.05; two-tailed t-test), performance and RF size were significantly anti-correlated in LI and LL (p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7B and statistical testing (two-tailed t-test).

claim: The ability of binary linear classifiers to linearly discriminate object pairs increased sharply as a function of population size N.
source: The ability of the classifiers to linearly discriminate the object pairs increased sharply as a function of N (Figure 8C, left).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8C, left.

claim: In LL, linear separability performance grew by approximately 500% when population size N increased from 6 to 96, reaching approximately 0.22 bits.
source: In LL, the performance grew of ~500%, when N increased from 6 to 96, reaching ~0.22 bits, which was nearly twice as large as the performance obtained in LI.
evidence: This is a direct report of the measured performance values from the experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: For a population of 96 neurons, LL linear separability performance (approximately 76% correct discrimination) was about 8 percentage points above LI, 10 above V1, and 17 above LM.
source: As a result, the differences among the areas became macroscopic – when measured in terms of classification accuracy (Figure 8C, right), LL performance (~76% correct discrimination) was about eight percentage points above LI, 10 above V1 and 17 above LM.
evidence: This is a direct report of the measured classification accuracy values from the experimental data shown in Figure 8C, right.

claim: For all object pairs tested, the linear separability performances yielded by LL were significantly larger than in any other area for populations of 96 neurons.
source: For all object pairs, the performances yielded by LL were significantly larger than in any other area (last column of Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D and described in the text.

claim: When measured in terms of accuracy for populations of 96 neurons, generalization performances in V1, LM and LI were barely above the 50% chance level, while in LL they approached 60% correct discrimination.
source: This implies a macroscopic advantage of LL, over the other areas, in terms of generalization ability – when measured in terms of accuracy (Figure 8E, right), the performances in V1, LM and LI were barely above the 50% chance level, while, in LL, they approached 60% correct discrimination.
evidence: This is a direct report of the measured classification accuracy values from the experimental data shown in Figure 8E, right.

claim: For all object pairs tested, the generalization performances yielded by LL were significantly larger than in any other area for populations of 96 neurons.
source: Again, the statistical significance of each pairwise area comparison was assessed at the level of the individual object pairs. For all the pairs, the performances yielded by LL were significantly larger than in any other area (last column of Figure 8F), while, for LI, the performances were significantly larger than in LM and V1 for two out of three pairs (middle column of Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 8F and described in the text.

claim: The findings provide compelling evidence about the existence of a ventral-like, object-processing pathway in rat visual cortex.
source: Taken together, these findings provide compelling evidence about the existence of a ventral-like, object-processing pathway in rat visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the totality of the experimental results presented in the study.

claim: V1, LI and LL belong to a cortical object-processing pathway, with V1 at the bottom of the functional hierarchy, LL at the top, and LI acting as an intermediate processing stage.
source: Because of this agreement, our results provide the strongest and most systematic functional evidence, to our knowledge, that V1, LI and LL belong to a cortical object-processing pathway, with V1 sitting at the bottom of the functional hierarchy, LL at the top, and LI acting as an intermediate processing stage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results and their agreement with primate ventral stream literature.

claim: LM never displayed any significant advantage over V1 in terms of higher-order processing of visual objects.
source: With regard to LM, our data do not support a clear assignment to the ventral stream, because this area never displayed any significant advantage, over V1, in terms of higher-order processing of visual objects.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing no significant differences between LM and V1.

claim: The significant increase of RF size and response latency from V1 to LM is consistent with LM being one step beyond V1 in the processing hierarchy.
source: Yet, the significant increase of RF size (Figure 7A) and response latency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) from V1 to LM is consistent with the role that mouse anatomical and functional studies have suggested for this area – one step beyond V1 in the processing hierarchy, routing both ventral and dorsal information, similar to area V2 in primates (Wang and Burkhalter, 2007; Wang et al., 2012; Glickfeld et al., 2014; Juavinett and Callaway, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and comparison with literature on mouse visual cortex.

claim: Rats were maintained in an anesthetized state during each recording session to allow for repeated presentation of a large number of stimulus conditions while maintaining good stability of recordings.
source: To allow for the repeated presentation (average of 26.5 trials per stimulus) of such large number of stimulus conditions, while maintaining a good stability of the recordings, rats were kept in an anesthetized state during each session (see Discussion for possible implications).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: The cortical area each unit was recorded from was identified by tracking the progression of the RFs recorded along a probe, so as to map the reversals of the retinotopy that delineate the borders between adjacent areas.
source: The cortical area each unit was recorded from was identified by tracking the progression of the RFs recorded along a probe (Figure 1C), so as to map the reversals of the retinotopy that, in rodent visual cortex, delineate the borders between adjacent areas (Schuett et al., 2002; Wang and Burkhalter, 2007; Andermann et al., 2011; Marshel et al., 2011; Polack and Contreras, 2012; Vermaercke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology, supported by citations to previous studies establishing this approach.

claim: The experimental design was inspired by a well-established approach in ventral stream studies, consisting in passively presenting an animal with a large number of visual objects in rapid sequence.
source: Our experimental design was inspired by a well-established approach in ventral stream studies, consisting in passively presenting an animal (either awake or anesthetized) with a large number of visual objects in rapid sequence.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design and its basis in established methodology.

claim: The passive viewing approach allows probing how object information is processed by the initial, largely feedforward cascade of ventral-stream computations underlying rapid recognition of visual objects.
source: This allows probing how object information is processed by the initial, largely feedforward cascade of ventral-stream computations underlying rapid recognition of visual objects (Thorpe et al., 1996; Fabre-Thorpe et al., 1998; Rousselet et al., 2002) – a reflexive, stimulus-driven process that is largely independent from top-down signals and whether the animal is engaged in a recognition task (DiCarlo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the experimental design, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Rapid recognition of visual objects is a reflexive, stimulus-driven process that is largely independent from top-down signals and whether the animal is engaged in a recognition task.
source: This allows probing how object information is processed by the initial, largely feedforward cascade of ventral-stream computations underlying rapid recognition of visual objects (Thorpe et al., 1996; Fabre-Thorpe et al., 1998; Rousselet et al., 2002) – a reflexive, stimulus-driven process that is largely independent from top-down signals and whether the animal is engaged in a recognition task (DiCarlo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of rapid visual recognition, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The stimulus set consisted of 10 visual objects and their transformations, for a total of 380 stimulus conditions.
source: During a recording session, a rat was presented with a rich battery of visual stimuli, consisting of 10 visual objects (Figure 1B, top), each transformed along five variation axes (Figure 1B, bottom), for a total of 380 stimulus conditions (i.e., object views).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: The stimulus conditions included combinations of object identities and transformations that have been previously shown to be invariantly recognized by rats.
source: These conditions included combinations of object identities (i.e., objects #7–10) and transformations that we have previously shown to be invariantly recognized by rats (Tafazoli et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the stimulus design, supported by a citation to a previous behavioral study.

claim: Drifting bars were used to map the receptive field of each recorded unit.
source: In addition, drifting bars were used to map the receptive field (RF) of each recorded unit (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Each stimulus condition was presented an average of 26.5 trials.
source: To allow for the repeated presentation (average of 26.5 trials per stimulus) of such large number of stimulus conditions, while maintaining a good stability of the recordings, rats were kept in an anesthetized state during each session (see Discussion for possible implications).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental design.

claim: The increase of invariant object information per neuron along the areas' progression does not imply that the total object information per area also increases.
source: Another important implication of our study concerns the increase of the invariant object information per neuron found across rat lateral visual areas (Figure 4C, bar plot). Critically, this finding does not imply that the overall invariant information per area also increases from V1 to LL.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from information theory principles and the anatomy of rat visual cortex.

claim: If the areas' progression acted as a purely feed-forward processing chain, a per area increase in information would violate the data processing inequality.
source: In fact, if the areas' progression acted as a purely feed-forward processing chain, a per area increase would mean that new object information is created from one processing step to the next, a fact that would violate the data processing inequality (Cover and Thomas, 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on information theory principles, supported by a citation.

claim: LM, LI and LL occupy a cortical surface that is, respectively, 31%, 3.5% and 2.1% of the surface of V1.
source: But in rat visual cortex, there is a strong reduction of the number of neurons from V1 through the succession of lateral extrastriate areas. LM, LI and LL occupy a cortical surface that is, respectively, 31%, 3.5% and 2.1% of the surface of V1 (Espinoza and Thomas, 1983).
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomy of rat visual cortex, supported by a citation.

claim: The connectivity among rat lateral visual areas is far from being strictly feed-forward.
source: In addition, the connectivity among rat lateral visual areas is far from being strictly feed-forward.
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomy of rat visual cortex, supported by citations in the following sentence.

claim: In both rats and mice, many corticortical and thalamocortical 'bypass' routes reach higher-level visual areas, in addition to the main anatomical route that connects consecutive processing stages step-by-step.
source: In both rats (Sanderson et al., 1991; Montero, 1993; Coogan and Burkhalter, 1993) and mice (Wang et al., 2012), many corticortical and thalamocortical 'bypass' routes reach higher-level visual areas, in addition to the main anatomical route that connects consecutive processing stages step-by-step (e.g., V1 directly projects to LI and LL, and LL receives direct projections from the thalamus).
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomy of rodent visual cortex, supported by citations.

claim: V1 directly projects to LI and LL in rodents.
source: In both rats (Sanderson et al., 1991; Montero, 1993; Coogan and Burkhalter, 1993) and mice (Wang et al., 2012), many corticortical and thalamocortical 'bypass' routes reach higher-level visual areas, in addition to the main anatomical route that connects consecutive processing stages step-by-step (e.g., V1 directly projects to LI and LL, and LL receives direct projections from the thalamus).
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomy of rodent visual cortex, given as an example of bypass routes.

claim: LL receives direct projections from the thalamus in rodents.
source: In both rats (Sanderson et al., 1991; Montero, 1993; Coogan and Burkhalter, 1993) and mice (Wang et al., 2012), many corticortical and thalamocortical 'bypass' routes reach higher-level visual areas, in addition to the main anatomical route that connects consecutive processing stages step-by-step (e.g., V1 directly projects to LI and LL, and LL receives direct projections from the thalamus).
evidence: This is a statement about the anatomy of rodent visual cortex, given as an example of bypass routes.

claim: The increase of invariant object information per neuron is likely an essential step to make information about object identity gradually more explicit and more easily readable by downstream neurons.
source: Rather, our interpretation is that the increase of invariant object information per neuron is likely an essential step to make information about object identity gradually more explicit, and more easily readable by downstream neurons that only have access to a limited number of presynaptic units (as confirmed by the linear decoding analyses shown in Figures 5–8).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, supported by the decoding analyses shown in Figures 5–8.

claim: The remarkable similarity between the anatomical organization of rat and mouse visual cortex suggests that mice can serve as powerful models to dissect ventral stream computations.
source: In addition, the remarkable similarity between the anatomical organization of rat and mouse visual cortex suggests that mice too can serve as powerful models to dissect ventral stream computations, given the battery of genetic and molecular tools that this species affords (Luo et al., 2008; Huberman and Niell, 2011; Katzner and Weigelt, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity between rat and mouse visual cortex anatomy and the availability of tools in mice, supported by citations.

claim: All animal procedures were approved by the Italian Ministry of Health.
source: All animal procedures were in agreement with international and institutional standards for the care and use of animals in research and were approved by the Italian Ministry of Health: project N. DGSAF 22791-A (submitted on Sep. 7, 2015) was approved on Dec. 10, 2015 (approval N. 1254/2015-PR); project N. 5388-III/14 (submitted on Aug. 23, 2012) and project N. 3612-III/12 (submitted on Sep. 15, 2009) were approved according to the legislative decree 116/92, article 7.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the ethical approval of the study.

claim: 26 naïve Long-Evans male rats were used in the study.
source: We used 26 naïve Long-Evans male rats (Charles River Laboratories), with age 3–12 months and weight 300–600 grams.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The rats used in the study were 3–12 months old and weighed 300–600 grams.
source: We used 26 naïve Long-Evans male rats (Charles River Laboratories), with age 3–12 months and weight 300–600 grams.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The rats were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of fentanyl and medetomidin.
source: The rats were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal (IP) injection of a solution of fentanyl (Fentanest: 0,3 mg/kg; Pfizer) and medetomidin (Domitor: 0,3 mg/kg; Orion Pharma).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Body temperature was maintained at 37.5°C by a feedback-controlled heating pad during recordings.
source: Body temperature was maintained at 37.5°C by a feedback-controlled heating pad (Panlab, Harvard Apparatus).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Heart rate and oxygen level were monitored through a pulse oximeter during recordings.
source: Heart rate and oxygen level were monitored through a pulse oximeter (Pulsesense-VET, Nonin), and a constant flow of oxygen was delivered to the rat to prevent hypoxia.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Recordings were performed with different configurations of 32-channel silicon probes.
source: Recordings were performed with different configurations of 32-channel silicon probes (NeuroNexus Technologies).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: For V1, the probe was inserted perpendicularly to the cortex.
source: For V1, the probe was inserted perpendicularly to the cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), while, for the lateral areas, it was tilted with an angle of ~30° (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: For the lateral areas, the probe was tilted with an angle of approximately 30°.
source: For V1, the probe was inserted perpendicularly to the cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), while, for the lateral areas, it was tilted with an angle of ~30° (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: The electrode was coated with Vybrant DiI cell-labeling solution before insertion to allow histological reconstruction of the electrode insertion track.
source: To allow the histological reconstruction of the electrode insertion track, the electrode was coated, before insertion, with Vybrant DiI cell-labeling solution (Life Technologies), and, at the end of the recording session, an electrolytic lesion was performed, by passing a 5 µA current for 2 s through the last 2 (multi-shank probes) or 4 (single-shank probe) channels at the tip of each shank (see below for a detailed description of the histological procedures).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: An electrolytic lesion was performed at the end of the recording session by passing a 5 µA current for 2 s through the last channels at the tip of each shank.
source: To allow the histological reconstruction of the electrode insertion track, the electrode was coated, before insertion, with Vybrant DiI cell-labeling solution (Life Technologies), and, at the end of the recording session, an electrolytic lesion was performed, by passing a 5 µA current for 2 s through the last 2 (multi-shank probes) or 4 (single-shank probe) channels at the tip of each shank (see below for a detailed description of the histological procedures).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: The aim was to record more than 100 units for each of the four visual areas under investigation.
source: Therefore, in our experiments, we aimed at recording more than 100 units for each of the four visual areas under investigation.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: Extracellular signals were acquired with a sampling rate of 25 kHz and were filtered from 0.3 to 5 kHz.
source: Extracellular signals were acquired using a system three workstation (Tucker-Davis Technologies) with a sampling rate of 25 kHz and were filtered from 0.3 to 5 kHz.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: Action potentials were detected and sorted for each recording site separately using Wave Clus.
source: Action potentials (spikes) were detected and sorted for each recording site separately, using Wave Clus (Quiroga et al., 2004) in MATLAB (The MathWorks).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology, with a citation to the spike sorting software.

claim: Neuronal responses were quantified by counting spikes in neuron-specific spike-count windows with a fixed duration of 150 ms.
source: Neuronal responses were quantified by counting spikes in neuron-specific spike-count windows (e.g., see gray patches in Figure 2A–B), with a fixed duration of 150 ms and an onset that was equal to the latency of the neuronal response, so as to capture most of the stimulus-evoked activity.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: The latency of neuronal response was estimated as the time when the response reached 20% of its peak value.
source: The latency was estimated as the time, relative to the stimulus onset, when the response reached 20% of its peak value [for a full description see (Zoccolan et al., 2007)].
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology, with a citation to a previous study.

claim: At the end of the recording session, each animal was deeply anesthetized with an overdose of urethane and perfused transcardially.
source: At the end of the recording session, each animal was deeply anesthetized with an overdose of urethane (1.5 gr/kg) and perfused transcardially with phosphate buffer saline (PBS) 0.1 M, followed by 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) in PBS 0.1 M, pH 7.4.
evidence: This is a direct description of the histological methodology.

claim: The brain was extracted and postfixed overnight in 4% PFA at 4°C.
source: The brain was extracted from the skull and postfixed overnight in 4% PFA at 4°C.
evidence: This is a direct description of the histological methodology.

claim: The tissue was cryoprotected by immersion in 15% w/v sucrose in PBS for at least 24 hr at 4°C, and then kept in 30% w/v sucrose in PBS.
source: After postfixation, the tissue was cryoprotected by immersion in 15% w/v sucrose in PBS 0.1 M for at least 24 hr at 4°C, and then kept in 30% w/v sucrose in PBS 0.1 M, until it was sectioned coronally at either 20 or 30 µm thickness on a freezing microtome (Leica SM2000R, Nussloch, Germany).
evidence: This is a direct description of the histological methodology.

claim: The tissue was sectioned coronally at either 20 or 30 µm thickness on a freezing microtome.
source: After postfixation, the tissue was cryoprotected by immersion in 15% w/v sucrose in PBS 0.1 M for at least 24 hr at 4°C, and then kept in 30% w/v sucrose in PBS 0.1 M, until it was sectioned coronally at either 20 or 30 µm thickness on a freezing microtome (Leica SM2000R, Nussloch, Germany).
evidence: This is a direct description of the histological methodology.

claim: For each slice, three different kinds of images were acquired: bright field photographs, fluorescence images, and Nissl-stained images.
source: For each slice, we acquired three different kinds of images, using a digital camera adapted to a Leica microscope (Leica DM6000B-CTR6000, Nussloch, Germany). First, various bright field photographs were taken at 2.5X and 10X magnification, so as to fully tile the region of the slice (left hemisphere) where the visual cortical areas were located. Second, for each of such bright field pictures, a matching fluorescence image was also acquired (using a red filter with emission at 700 nm), to visualize the red fluorescence track left by the insertion of the probe (that had been coated with Vybrant DiI cell-labeling solution before the insertion) (DiCarlo et al., 1996; Blanche et al., 2005). Following the acquisition of this set of images, the slices were further stained for Nissl substance (using the Cresyl Violet method) and pictures were taken at 2.5X and 10X magnification.
evidence: This is a direct description of the histological methodology.

claim: The fluorescence, bright field, and Nissl-stained images were processed using Inkscape to reconstruct the anteroposterior coordinate of the probe insertion track and the laminar location of the recording sites.
source: The fluorescence, bright field, and Nissl-stained images were processed using Inkscape (an open source SVG editor; http://www.inkscape.org), so as to reconstruct the anteroposterior coordinate of the probe insertion track and, when possible, the laminar location of the recording sites along the probe.
evidence: This is a direct description of the histological methodology.

claim: The boundaries between the cortical layers were identified based on the difference in size, morphology and density of the Nissl-labeled cells across the cortical thickness.
source: In the final image, the boundaries between the cortical layers (red lines in Figure 1—figure supplement 1) were identified, based on the difference in size, morphology and density of the Nissl-labeled cells across the cortical thickness.
evidence: This is a direct description of the histological methodology.

claim: In the analyses, units recorded from layers II/III and IV were grouped together, and those recorded from layers V and VI were grouped together.
source: Since the number of neurons sampled from each individual cortical layer was not very large, in our analyses, we grouped the units recorded from layers II/III and IV and those recorded from layers V and VI (see Figure 6C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: The stimulus set consisted of 380 visual object conditions, obtained by producing 38 distinct views of 10 different objects.
source: Our stimulus set consisted of 380 visual object conditions, obtained by producing 38 distinct views (or transformations) of 10 different objects, using the ray tracer POV-Ray (http://www.povray.org/).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Six of the objects were computer-graphics reproductions of real-world objects, while the remaining four were artificial shapes originally designed for a behavioral study.
source: Six of them (#1–6) were computer-graphics reproductions of real-world objects, while the remaining four (#7–10) were artificial shapes, originally designed for a behavioral study assessing invariant visual object recognition in rats (Tafazoli et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli, with a citation to the behavioral study.

claim: Each object was horizontally shifted across the stimulus display from −22.5° to +30° of visual angle in steps of 7.5°.
source: Positions changes: each object was horizontally shifted across the stimulus display, from −22.5° to +30° of visual angle (azimuth), in steps of 7.5° (Figure 1B.1).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Each object was scaled from 15° to 55° of visual angle in steps of 10°.
source: Size changes: each object was scaled from 15° to 55° of visual angle, in steps of 10° (Figure 1B.2).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Each object was in-plane rotated from −40° to +40° in steps of 20°.
source: In-plane rotations: each object was in-plane rotated from −40° to +40°, in steps of 20° (Figure 1B.3).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Each object was presented at five different in-depth rotation angles: −60°, −40°, 0°, +40°, and +60°.
source: In-depth rotations: each object was presented at five different in-depth (azimuth) rotation angles: −60°, −40°, 0°, + 40°, and +60° (Figure 1B.4).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Each object was presented at four different luminance levels: 100%, 50%, 25% and 12.5%.
source: Luminance changes: each object was presented at four different luminance levels: 100% (i.e., default luminance), 50%, 25% and 12.5% (Figure 1B.5).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: The object conditions were presented in rapid sequence (250 ms stimulus on, followed by 250 ms of blank screen), randomly interleaved with drifting bars.
source: The object conditions were presented in rapid sequence (250 ms stimulus on, followed by 250 ms of blank screen), randomly interleaved with the drifting bars used to map the neuronal RFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: For V1 neurons, each condition was presented on average 26 ± 2 times.
source: For V1 neurons, each conditions was presented, on average, 26 ± 2 times; for LM neurons, 25 ± 4 times; for LI neurons, 27 ± 3 times; and for LL, neurons 28 ± 2 times.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental design.

claim: For LM neurons, each condition was presented on average 25 ± 4 times.
source: For V1 neurons, each conditions was presented, on average, 26 ± 2 times; for LM neurons, 25 ± 4 times; for LI neurons, 27 ± 3 times; and for LL, neurons 28 ± 2 times.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental design.

claim: For LI neurons, each condition was presented on average 27 ± 3 times.
source: For V1 neurons, each conditions was presented, on average, 26 ± 2 times; for LM neurons, 25 ± 4 times; for LI neurons, 27 ± 3 times; and for LL, neurons 28 ± 2 times.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental design.

claim: For LL neurons, each condition was presented on average 28 ± 2 times.
source: For V1 neurons, each conditions was presented, on average, 26 ± 2 times; for LM neurons, 25 ± 4 times; for LI neurons, 27 ± 3 times; and for LL, neurons 28 ± 2 times.
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental design.

claim: The stimuli were displayed on a 47 inch LCD monitor with 1920 × 1080 pixel resolution, 60 Hz refresh rate, 9 ms response time, 700 cd/m2 maximum brightness, and 1.200:1 contrast ratio.
source: The stimuli were displayed on a 47 inch LCD monitor (Sharp PN-E471R), with 1920 × 1080 pixel resolution, 60 Hz refresh rate, 9 ms response time, 700 cd/m2 maximum brightness, 1.200:1 contrast ratio, positioned at a distance of 30 cm from the right eye, spanning a visual field of 120° azimuth and 90° elevation.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental setup.

claim: The monitor was positioned at a distance of 30 cm from the right eye, spanning a visual field of 120° azimuth and 90° elevation.
source: The stimuli were displayed on a 47 inch LCD monitor (Sharp PN-E471R), with 1920 × 1080 pixel resolution, 60 Hz refresh rate, 9 ms response time, 700 cd/m2 maximum brightness, 1.200:1 contrast ratio, positioned at a distance of 30 cm from the right eye, spanning a visual field of 120° azimuth and 90° elevation.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental setup.

claim: To avoid distortions of the objects' shape, the stimuli were presented under a tangent screen projection.
source: To avoid distortions of the objects' shape, the stimuli were presented under a tangent screen projection (see next section and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental methodology.

claim: The optimal viewing distance for rats has been reported to range between 20 and 30 cm.
source: This number was chosen, because the optimal viewing distance for rats has been reported to range between 20 and 30 cm (Wiesenfeld and Branchek, 1976).
evidence: This is a statement about rat vision, supported by a citation.

claim: Rats are capable of discriminating complex visual objects under a variety of identity-preserving transformations when viewing the objects at a distance of 30 cm.
source: In addition, earlier behavioral studies from our group have shown that rats are capable of discriminating complex visual objects under a variety of identity-preserving transformations, when viewing the objects at a distance of 30 cm (Zoccolan et al., 2009; Tafazoli et al., 2012; Alemi-Neissi et al., 2013; Rosselli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about rat behavior, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The tangent screen projection allows presenting the stimuli as they would appear if they were shown on virtual screens that are tangent to a circle centered on the rat's eye.
source: This projection allows presenting the stimuli as they would appear, if they were shown on virtual screens that are tangent to a circle centered on the rat's eye, with a radius equal to the distance from the eye to the point on the display just in front of it (i.e., 30 cm).
evidence: This is a direct description of the tangent screen projection methodology.

claim: Thanks to the tangent screen projection, the shape, size and aspect ratio of each stimulus were preserved across all eight azimuth positions tested.
source: Thanks to this projection, the shape, size and aspect ratio of each stimulus were preserved across all the eight azimuth positions tested in our experiment (see previous section).
evidence: This is a direct description of the effect of the tangent screen projection.

claim: Data analysis was restricted to neurons that were visually driven and stimulus informative.
source: Throughout our study, data analysis was restricted to those neurons that met two criteria: (1) being visually driven; and (2) being stimulus informative.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: A neuron was considered visually driven if at least one stimulus condition evoked a response that was significantly different from background (p<0.05 with Bonferroni correction).
source: The first criterion was implemented as following. Given a neuron, its response to each of the 380 object conditions and its background firing rate were computed. A 2-tailed t-test was then applied to check if at least one of these conditions evoked a response that was significantly different (either larger or lower) than background (p<0.05 with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparison).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: A neuron was considered stimulus informative if it carried a significant amount of information I(R;S) (p<0.05; permutation test).
source: The second criterion was based on the computation of the mutual information between stimulus and response I(R;S) (defined below). Note that, in this case, only 230 object conditions S were used (see next section). To be included in the analysis, a neuron had to carry a significant amount of information I(R;S) (p<0.05; permutation test; described below).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: For any given neuron, all eight positions were included in the single-cell mutual information and decoding analyses, while of the remaining transformations, only those shown at the position closer to the neuron's RF center were used.
source: For any given neuron, all the eight positions were included in the single-cell mutual information and decoding analyses (Figures 3–7), while, of the remaining transformations, only those shown at the position that was closer to the neuron's RF center (i.e., either −15° or +15°) were used.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: This yielded 23 different transformations per object, for a total of 230 stimuli S used in single-cell analyses.
source: This yielded 23 different transformations per object, for a total of 230 stimuli S.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: In the population decoding analyses, 19 of the 23 transformations per object were used.
source: In the case of the population decoding analyses (Figure 8), 19 of these 23 transformations per object were used (see below).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: A fit of the RF map was considered acceptable if the coefficient of determination R2 was larger than 0.5.
source: A fit was considered acceptable if R2 was larger than 0.5.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: RF luminance was defined as the dot product between the raw RF map of the neuron and the luminance profile of the stimulus over the image plane.
source: To estimate how much luminous energy any given stimulus (i.e., object condition) impinged on a neuronal RF, we defined a metric (which we called RF luminance), resulting from computing the dot product between the raw RF map of the neuron (normalized to its maximal value, so as to range between 0 and 1) and the luminance profile of the stimulus over the image plane.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: RF contrast was defined as the standard deviation of the RF-weighted luminance values produced by the stimulus that were contained within the RF itself.
source: A similar approach was used to measure the variability of the pattern of luminance impinged by a stimulus on a neuronal RF, using a metric that we called RF contrast. This metric was defined as the standard deviation of the RF-weighted luminance values produced by the stimulus that were contained within the RF itself (see the rightmost plot in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: In the RF contrast analysis, only object conditions that covered at least 10% of the RFs were considered.
source: Therefore, in the analysis in which we assessed the amount of information carried by single neurons about RF contrast (Figure 3—figure supplement 4), we only considered object conditions that covered at least 10% of the RFs.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: Refractory violations (RV) was defined as the fraction of inter spike intervals that were shorter than 2 ms.
source: RV was defined as the fraction of inter spike intervals (ISI) that were shorter than 2 ms, the rationale being that a large RV indicates a substantial violation of the neuron's refractory period and, therefore, a contamination from other units (Hill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology, with a citation.

claim: All single-cell properties measured for the visual areas have been reported in terms of medians ± Standard Error of the median estimated by bootstrap.
source: All the single-cell properties measured for the visual areas have been reported in terms of medians ± Standard Error (SE) of the median (estimated by bootstrap).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis and reporting methodology.

claim: The statistical significance of each pairwise, between-area comparison was assessed with a 1-tailed, Mann-Whitney U-test, with Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
source: In all these cases, the statistical significance of each pairwise, between-area comparison was assessed with a 1-tailed, Mann-Whitney U-test, with Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
evidence: This is a direct description of the statistical methodology.

claim: The choice of the 1-tailed test was motivated by the fact that there was a clear hypothesis about the rank of each visual area based on previous studies.
source: The choice of the 1-tailed test was motivated by the fact that, in any comparison, we had a clear hypothesis about the rank of each visual area, with respect to the measured property, based on previous anatomical, lesion and functional studies (see Introduction and Discussion).
evidence: This is a direct explanation of the statistical methodology choice.

claim: In all information theoretic analyses, the response R was quantified as the number of spikes fired by a neuron in a 150 ms-wide spike count window, discretized into three equi-populated bins.
source: In all the information theoretic analyses, the response R was quantified as the number of spikes fired by a neuron in a 150 ms-wide spike count window (see above), discretized into three equi-populated bins (whose boundaries were computed, for each neuron independently, on the whole set of responses collected across repeated presentations of all the stimuli).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: The discretization into three response bins yielded about nine trials per stimulus per response bin.
source: Given that we recorded an average of 26.5 trials per stimulus (see above), this discretization yielded about nine trials per stimulus per response bin.
evidence: This is a direct calculation based on the experimental design.

claim: Earlier studies showed that limited sampling bias in information calculations can be effectively corrected if there are at least four repetitions per stimulus and per response bin.
source: Earlier studies (Panzeri and Treves, 1996; Panzeri et al., 2007) showed that the limited sampling bias in information calculations can be effectively corrected out – leading to precise information estimations – if there are at least four repetitions per stimulus and per response bin.
evidence: This is a statement about information theory methodology, supported by citations.

claim: For the computation of RF luminance information, L was discretized in 23 bins.
source: Since, for each object and neuron, the maximum number of possible luminance values L is equal to the number of unique transformations the objet underwent (i.e., 23), L was discretized in 23 bins (see Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: This number of luminance bins fully covered the luminance variation for each object without loss of luminance information and yielded on average 100 trials per response and stimulus bin.
source: This number of luminance bins fully covered the luminance variation for each object, without loss of luminance information, and it yielded, on average, 100 trials per response and stimulus bin, which was comfortably sufficient to control for the sampling bias in the computation of the mutual information (Panzeri et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology and its justification, with a citation.

claim: To evaluate the statistical significance of mutual information values, a random permutation method was used.
source: To evaluate the statistical significance of mutual information values we used a random permutation method (Ince et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct description of the statistical methodology, with a citation.

claim: In the random permutation method, the association between stimulus and response was randomly permuted 100 times to generate a null-hypothesis distribution of information values.
source: In this method, separately for each considered information calculation and for each neuron, the association between stimulus and response was randomly permuted 100 times, to generate a null-hypothesis distribution of information values in the absence of any association between stimulus and response.
evidence: This is a direct description of the statistical methodology.

claim: All information measures were corrected for limited sampling bias using the Panzeri-Treves method.
source: All information measures were computed using the Information Breakdown Toolbox (Magri et al., 2009) and were corrected for limited sampling bias using the Panzeri-Treves method (Panzeri and Treves, 1996; Panzeri et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology, with citations.

claim: The Panzeri-Treves method uses an asymptotic large-N expansion to estimate and subtract out the limited sampling bias from the raw information estimate.
source: This method uses an asymptotic large-N expansion (where N is the total number of trials available across all stimuli) to estimate and then subtract out the limited sampling bias from the raw information estimate.
evidence: This is a direct description of the bias correction methodology.

claim: The test of linear separability was carried out following a 5-fold cross-validation procedure.
source: This analysis was carried out following a 5-fold cross-validation procedure.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: The performance of the single-cell decoder was computed as the mutual information between the actual and the predicted object labels from the decoding outcomes.
source: As explained in the Results, the performance was computed as the mutual information between the actual and the predicted object labels from the decoding outcomes [i.e., as the mutual information between the rows and columns of the confusion matrix (Quiroga and Panzeri, 2009)].
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology, with a citation.

claim: For each object pair in the generalization analysis, the procedure was repeated 1000 times, with the training transformations randomly sampled in each run.
source: For each object pair, this procedure was repeated 1000 times. In each of these runs, the training transformations of the two objects were randomly sampled, so as to span a wide range of training and testing object views.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: In the test of generalization along parametric size changes, decoders were trained to discriminate two objects at a given size and then tested for their ability to generalize when those same objects were shown at either smaller or larger sizes.
source: A similar kind of analysis was performed for the transformations along the size axis (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1B). The cross-validation procedure was similar to the one described in the previous paragraph for the position changes. However, since the size conditions were fewer than the position ones (Figure 1B, bottom), and lent themselves to be analyzed in terms of generalization from small to larger sizes (and vice versa), we grouped them into three classes: (1) the default size (i.e., 35°); (2) the two sizes than were smaller than 35° (i.e., 15° and 25°); and 3) the two sizes than were larger than 35° (i.e., 45° and 55°). Given an object pair, we tested all possible generalizations from the default size to the smaller and larger sizes and, vice versa.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: Chance performances in the single-cell decoding analyses were obtained by randomly permuting the object identity labels associated to the responses before building the decoder.
source: In the cross-validation procedures described above (for both the tests of linear separability and generalization), each step yielding a classification performance also yielded a chance generalization performance. This was computed by randomly permuting the object identity labels associated to the responses of the neuron before building the decoder.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: Chance performances were subtracted from actual classification performances to obtain conservative estimates of transformation-tolerance.
source: First, to obtain conservative estimates of the ability of the decoders to generalize to new object views, the chance performances were subtracted from the actual (i.e., un-shuffled) classification performances.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: The distribution of classification performances obtained for a neuronal population was compared to the matching distribution of chance performances to assess statistical significance.
source: Second, the distribution of classification performances obtained for a neuronal population was compared to the matching distribution of chance performances, to assess whether the former was significantly larger than the latter (according to a 1-tailed, Mann-Whitney U-test).
evidence: This is a direct description of the statistical methodology.

claim: In the population decoding analysis, subpopulations of 6, 12, 24, 48 and 96 units were randomly sampled from the full sets of neurons recorded in each area.
source: Following the design of previous population decoding studies of the monkey ventral stream (Hung et al., 2005; Rust and Dicarlo, 2010; Pagan et al., 2013), we measured whether (and how sharply) the decoders' performance grew as a function of the size of the neuronal populations, by randomly sampling subpopulations of 6, 12, 24, 48 and 96 units from the full sets of neurons recorded in each area.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology, with citations to previous studies.

claim: Pseudo-population response vectors were built by assigning to each component the response of the corresponding neuron in a randomly sampled presentation of the stimulus.
source: Since the neurons belonging to each area were recorded across different sessions (and, therefore, not all the neurons in a given area were recorded simultaneously; see Figure 1—source data 1), the pseudo-population response vectors to stimulus S were built by assigning to each component of the vector the response of the corresponding neuron in a randomly sampled presentation of S.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: A Support Vector Machine with a linear kernel was used as the decoder in the population decoding analysis.
source: As a decoder, we used a Support Vector Machine (SVM) (Cristianini and Shawe-Taylor, 2000) in its Matlab implementation, with a linear kernel.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology, with a citation.

claim: The specific method used to find the hyperplane in the population decoding analysis was Sequential Minimal Optimization.
source: The specific method used to find the hyperplane was Sequential Minimal Optimization (SMO) (Schölkopf and Smola, 2001).
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology, with a citation.

claim: The soft-margin parameter C was set to its default value of 1 for all trainings in the population decoding analysis.
source: The soft-margin parameter C was set to its default value of 1 for all the trainings.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: In the population decoding analysis, a 5-fold cross-validation procedure was used for the test of linear separability.
source: As in the case of the single-cell analysis, we applied a 5-fold cross-validation procedure.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: Chance classification performances in the population decoding analysis were obtained by randomly shuffling the association between object identity labels and pseudo-population response vectors.
source: As in the case of the single-cell analyses, we also computed chance classification performances (for both the tests of linear separability and generalization). These were obtained by running the same decoding analyses described above, but with the key difference of randomly shuffling first the association between object identity labels and pseudo-population response vectors.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: For the population decoding analysis, chance performances were subtracted from actual performances only for results reported as mutual information, not for results reported as classification accuracy.
source: This subtraction was done only for the performances computed as the mutual information between the actual and the predicted object labels from the decoding outcomes (i.e., results shown in Figure 8C and E, left and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B, left). For the results reported in terms of classification accuracy (Figure 8C and E, right and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B, right), the chance performances were not subtracted from the actual performances, so as to better highlight that the theoretical chance level was 50% correct discrimination.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis and reporting methodology.

claim: The chance performances in the population decoding analysis were all between 49.4% and 50.1% correct discrimination for the linear separability test.
source: These chance performances were all between 49.4% and 50.1% correct discrimination for the linear separability test, and between 49.98% and 50.02% correct discrimination for the generalization test.
evidence: This is a direct report of the measured chance performance values.

claim: The chance performances in the population decoding analysis were all between 49.98% and 50.02% correct discrimination for the generalization test.
source: These chance performances were all between 49.4% and 50.1% correct discrimination for the linear separability test, and between 49.98% and 50.02% correct discrimination for the generalization test.
evidence: This is a direct report of the measured chance performance values.

claim: For neurons with RF center closer to −15°, the rightmost four positions (from +7.5° to +30°) were excluded from the population decoding analysis.
source: In fact, for the neurons with RF center that was closer to −15°, the rightmost four positions (i.e., from +7.5° to +30° of visual angle) were excluded.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: For neurons with RF center closer to +15°, the leftmost four positions (from −22.5° to 0°) were excluded from the population decoding analysis.
source: Similarly, for the neurons with RF center that was closer to +15°, the leftmost four positions (i.e., from −22.5° to 0° of visual angle) were excluded.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.

claim: The exclusion of certain positions in the population decoding analysis allowed aligning the two groups of neuronal RFs by mapping complementary position ranges onto each other.
source: As a result, for the group of neurons with RFs closer to the −15° position, the 19 chosen transformations were the complementary set of the 19 transformations chosen for the group of neurons with RFs closer to the +15° position. This allowed aligning the two groups of neuronal RFs, by mapping the [−22.5°, 0°] range of positions of the first group onto the [ + 7.5°,+30°] range of positions of the second one, thus obtaining a single neuronal population, from which the neurons in each resampling iteration could be drawn.
evidence: This is a direct description of the data analysis methodology.
